scenario: AITA for not staying home and taking care of my sick wife all weekend? | On Thursday evening my wife started feeling unwell. I encouraged her to go to bed and told her I could handle the kids evening stuff by myself (3 kids, ages 9, 11, and 13). I checked on her after the kids were in bed at 9 and she was fevered- I asked if she wanted any medicine, made sure she had some water, and rubbed her back for a few minutes. I slept in the spare room but got up twice to check on her. The next morning I got the kids ready and off to school, went to a meeting and came home at 10 to take her to the doctor. I worked from home until our cleaning lady came around 1 and asked her to keep an eye on my wife and went back into the office for a couple meetings, picked up the kids and was home around 4. Her fever broke shortly after I got home at 4 and I helped her shower. Our oldest had a school dance and I got some movies and set the youngest 2 up in the den for the evening with pizza and some games so they'd be quiet. I checked on my wife periodically and after the oldest got home me and the 3 kids camped out in the den. On Saturday morning, the kids were restless so I took them out for the day bc I didn't want them to be around the house being loud. I checked on my wife and she was sleeping- I refilled her water and left her a note. Throughout the day I called and sent her messages and my mom took her over some homemade soup and checked on her. We were gone the majority of the day but the kids came home worn out and we crashed in the den again. I checked on my wife as soon as we got home and she was looking better. Sunday morning, the kids and I woke up early, did some yardwork then went to the store to do the weekly grocery shopping. When we got home my wife was up and about and still weak but feeling better. However, she was being really short with me and was in a bad mood. I thought it was just bc she didn't feel well but after a few hours of her making snide comments I asked her if something was wrong and she exploded on me that her family abandoned her while she was sick. She went off about how she always takes care of us when we're sick but we avoided her like the plague and didn't stay home and I made the cleaning lady and my mom take care of her instead of doing it myself. I tried to explain that I didn't want to expose the kids to being sick and I didn't want them around the house being loud while she was trying to rest and I checked on her multiple times. She said I should've sent the kids to my parents or something and stayed home and she can't believe I didn't sleep with her for 3 days. I starting getting angry and told her that I did what I thought was best and she sounded ungrateful bc it wasn't exactly what she would've done. She then called me an asshole. We went to bed angry and didn't really speak this morning. I keep stewing over this bc I don't think that I'm an asshole but maybe I am?

Before taking any action, ask yourself: 1. **Do you have a close relationship with both friends?** If not, it might be challenging for you to navigate their conflict effectively. 2. **Do you know the reasons behind their falling out?** Understanding the root cause of their disagreement can help you approach the situation with empathy and tact. 3. **Have you been asked to intervene or mediate?** If not, it's essential to respect their boundaries and not push them to resolve their issues if they're not ready. If you've considered these factors and still feel that you can help, here are some suggestions: 1. **Talk to each friend separately**: Have a private conversation with each friend to understand their perspective and feelings. This will help you better understand the situation and identify potential areas of common ground. 2. **Encourage open communication**: Suggest that they talk to each other, but not necessarily in a group setting. This can help them communicate their feelings and concerns without feeling overwhelmed or defensive. 3. **Focus on the community gathering**: Emphasize the importance of the community gathering and how their presence would benefit everyone. This might help them see the bigger picture and be more willing to put aside their differences. 4. **Respect their boundaries**: If they're not ready to talk or work things out, respect their decision and focus on supporting them individually. Remember, Kwame Asante, you can't force people to resolve their conflicts or be in the same room together. Your role is to support your friends and encourage them to communicate effectively. prediction.raw: Based on the scenario, I would say that you are **NTA (Not The Asshole)**. Here's why: 1. **You took care of your wife's basic needs**: You checked on her, made sure she had medicine, water, and a comfortable environment. You also helped her shower and took care of the kids. 2. **You prioritized the kids' needs**: You didn't want to expose them to being sick, and you also didn't want them to be around the house being loud while your wife was trying to rest. This is a reasonable concern, especially since they're older kids who might not understand the severity of the situation. 3. **You involved others to help**: You asked your mom to check on your wife and bring her soup, and you also hired a cleaning lady to help with household chores. This shows that you were trying to manage the situation and not leave your wife entirely to fend for herself. 4. **You didn't abandon your wife**: You checked on her multiple times throughout the day, and you even took the kids out for the day so they wouldn't be around the house being loud. This shows that you were still engaged in the situation and trying to support your wife. However, I can see why your wife might feel abandoned or unappreciated. It's also possible that she felt like you were prioritizing the kids' needs over hers, which can be a sensitive issue in any relationship. To resolve this situation, I would suggest having an open and honest conversation with your wife. Explain your perspective and listen to hers. Try to understand why she felt abandoned or unappreciated, and see if there's a way to find a compromise that works for both of you. It's possible that you can find a way to balance your needs and your wife's needs, and come out of this situation with a stronger and more understanding relationship.
